Volume 13 · Chapter 05

Welfare, aggregation and social choice

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c04

By the endProve welfare results and assess aggregation and distributional restrictions.

Volume 13 · Chapter 5

Welfare, aggregation and social choice

A market allocation can be efficient without being equitable. A price vector can support a desired allocation without making every household choose it. Aggregate demand can ignore redistribution without identifying whose welfare should count more. These distinctions become sharper, rather than disappear, when collective choice is formalized.

Capability. Prove the welfare theorems with their different hypotheses; construct ownership-consistent transfers and diagnose quasiequilibrium; establish exact income aggregation on a declared domain; solve explicit social objectives; and prove a finite Arrow impossibility theorem rather than mistaking a majority cycle for its proof. The six worked cases and twelve solved exercises are original, synthetic mathematical economies and voting profiles.

Prerequisites. Preference representation fixes weak orders and ordinal meaning, duality supplies demand and global optimization tools, and uncertainty and information proves compact finite separation. General equilibrium and existence defines private-ownership production economies and establishes an explicitly scoped existence theorem. We condition welfare claims on the existence of the stated allocations and equilibria; the stronger separation lemma needed for unbounded resource sets is proved here.

1. Prices, resources and the first welfare theorem

There are finitely many households i=1,…,I and L commodities. Household i has a nonempty consumption set Xi⊆ℝ+L, endowment ωi≥0, and a complete, transitive preference ≽i over its own bundle. There are finitely many firms j with nonempty sets Yj⊆ℝL of net outputs: inputs are negative coordinates. The no-firm case uses an empty sum equal to zero. Ownership shares θij≥0 obey Σiθij=1 for every firm. Let ω=Σωi. With free disposal, feasibility means xi∈Xi, yj∈Yj, and Σxi≤ω+Σyj coordinatewise. A Pareto improvement makes every household weakly better off and at least one strictly better off; an allocation is Pareto efficient if no such feasible improvement exists.

Prices p≥0 are nonzero. At a competitive equilibrium with fixed lump-sum transfers τi, firms maximize p·y on their entire technologies, transfers balance Στi=0, and each household maximizes its preference on p·x≤wi, where

wi=p·ωi+Σjθijp·yj*+τi.

The allocation is feasible and disposed resources have zero value, p·(ω+Σyj*−Σxi*)=0. Transfers redistribute purchasing power in these commodity units; the theorem presumes the authority and trading opportunities to implement them. They are not new aggregate resources. With no transfers set every τi=0.

First welfare theorem. If household preferences are locally nonsatiated relative to their Xi, every such equilibrium is Pareto efficient. Neither convexity nor differentiability is required. Local nonsatiation means that arbitrarily close to every x∈Xi is a strictly preferred feasible consumption point in Xi. First, any x≽ixi* must cost at least wi. Otherwise its strictly positive budget slack leaves a relative neighborhood affordable, since p·x is continuous; local nonsatiation supplies a nearby point strictly preferred to x and hence to the equilibrium choice, a contradiction. Any x≻ixi* must cost strictly more than wi, directly by budget optimality. This distinction between weak and strict preference is essential.

If a feasible Pareto improvement (x′,y′) existed, summing those inequalities would give

p·Σx′i > Σwi = p·ω+Σp·yj* ≥ p·ω+Σp·y′j ≥ p·Σx′i.

Ownership and balanced transfers give the equality, firm optimality gives the first weak inequality, and nonnegative prices plus feasibility give the last. This contradiction proves the result. The same local-slack argument also proves each equilibrium household exhausts its budget. No interpersonal comparison of utilities appears. The hypothesis that preferences concern the modeled own bundle rules out an omitted external effect; completeness of the relevant commodity opportunities cannot simply be assumed when applying the theorem to an institution.

Worked case 1: an efficient exchange and an omitted effect

Two households have endowments (5,1) and (1,5). Their utilities are u₁=x₁1/3x₂2/3 and u₂=x₁2/3x₂1/3. At p=(1,1), incomes are (6,6) and demands are ((2,4),(4,2)), exactly using aggregate endowment (6,6). More generally, for positive prices and income m, maximizing x₁αx₂1−α, 0<α<1, gives (αm/p₁,(1−α)m/p₂). To see global optimality, spend the whole budget and write the expenditure share on good 1 as s; αlog s+(1−α)log(1−s) is strictly concave, has its unique maximum at s=α, and the boundary product is zero. Local nonsatiation and the first theorem therefore establish efficiency here. The individual utility values both have cube 32, but equal utility labels are not a statement of interpersonal equality.

A separate two-good example shows why an omitted effect matters. Goods are money m and an emitting consumption q. Household A owns (0,3), B owns (6,0), and prices are (1,2). A values mA+2qA; B values mB−3qA. Treating qA as given, B spends its income on money; A is indifferent among its budget-line bundles and chooses (0,3). B chooses (6,0), markets clear, and utilities are (6,-3). But B can transfer 2 money units to A while A cuts emitting consumption to 2. Bundles become (2,2) and (4,0), with one unit of q discarded, and utilities become (6,-2). The transfer balances and physical resources suffice, so this is a Pareto improvement. These private choices are not an equilibrium satisfying the theorem’s own-bundle preference hypothesis: B’s utility depends on A’s consumption. No welfare contradiction arises.

The first-theorem value argument and ownership accounting build on the previously inspected MIT welfare lecture. The cases and the explicit hypothesis audit are original.

2. The separation theorem needed for welfare support

The compact nearest-point lemma from C03 does not directly separate an open, possibly unbounded set of improvements from a possibly unbounded resource set. We prove the required finite-dimensional extension. Throughout this section all interiors and closures are in the ambient Euclidean space.

Interior-segment fact. If D is nonempty open convex, d∈D, z∈cl D and 0<λ≤1, then λd+(1−λ)z∈D. For λ=1 this is immediate. Otherwise choose a ball B(d,r)⊂D and zn∈D approaching z. For large n, dn=d+(1−λ)(z−zn)/λ lies in that ball, and λdn+(1−λ)zn=λd+(1−λ)z belongs to D by convexity. The same construction with small perturbations gives a neighborhood inside D.

Open-convex separation lemma. If D⊂ℝL is nonempty open convex and 0∉D, there is a nonzero p with p·d≥0 for all d∈D. To prove it, set K=cl D, a nonempty closed convex set. Every external point z has a nearest point c∈K even if K is unbounded: a minimizing sequence can be restricted to a closed bounded ball by comparison with any fixed point of K, and a convergent subsequence attains the distance. Differentiating ‖z−[c+t(k−c)]‖² at t=0 along K gives (c−z)·(k−c)≥0 for every k∈K.

If 0∉K, take z=0 and p=c/‖c‖; then p·k≥‖c‖>0. If 0∈K but 0∉D, choose d₀∈D and zn=−d₀/n. Every zn is outside K: otherwise the interior-segment fact applied to d₀ and zn would put 0 in D. For their nearest points cn, the feasibility of 0∈K gives ‖cn−zn‖≤‖zn‖ and therefore cn→0. Normalize pn=(cn−zn)/‖cn−zn‖. A subsequence on the compact unit sphere converges to a unit p, and the nearest-point inequality passes to p·k≥0 for every fixed k∈K. The same subsequence works because each inequality held for every k. This completes the proof. In fact p·d>0 for d∈D, since an interior point with zero value could be moved a little in direction −p while remaining in D.

Consequently, if nonempty convex sets S,A are disjoint and A is open, apply the lemma to D=S−A. This set is open and convex, and excludes zero; we obtain p·s≥p·a for every s∈S,a∈A. No compactness or closedness of S or A is assumed. Where A is only known to have dense interior, the inequality extends to all of A by limits. The proof has supplied precisely this input, not an infinite-dimensional separation theorem.

3. Second welfare support, transfers and the missing upgrade

Now assume each Xi⊆ℝ+L is nonempty convex; preferences are complete, transitive, continuous relative to Xi, locally nonsatiated there, and have convex weak upper contour sets. Each Yj is nonempty convex. Closedness, compactness, differentiability and strictly positive endowments are not required for this support statement, which starts with a specified feasible Pareto-efficient allocation (x*,y*). Feasibility continues to allow free disposal. These assumptions are distinct from a theorem guaranteeing that an efficient allocation or a competitive equilibrium exists.

Write Pi={x∈Xi:x≻ixi*}. It is nonempty by local nonsatiation and convex: between two strictly better points, choose the weakly less preferred one; both are in its convex weak upper contour, which still lies strictly above xi*. Local nonsatiation also gives xi*∈cl Pi. The set Pi is relatively open, but need not be open in ℝL. We therefore use the resource side for ambient openness.

S=ΣiPi,   A=ω+ΣjYj−ℝ+L,   z*=Σixi*.

S and A are nonempty convex and disjoint, since an intersection would finance a strict improvement for every household. The resource set A is downward closed and has a nonempty ambient interior: for any a∈A and ε>0, a−ε1 has a small ball below a coordinatewise. These interior points approach every a∈A, so A⊆cl(int A). Separate S from int A by Section 2 and extend to A. This yields nonzero p with p·s≥p·a for every s∈S,a∈A. Downward closure forces p≥0: if pℓ<0, points a−teℓ would have arbitrarily large value, contradicting the bound from any fixed s.

Local nonsatiation gives z*∈cl S, while feasibility gives z*∈A. Taking limits in the inequality shows that z* maximizes p·a over A. Put a*=ω+Σyj*; then a*∈A and a*≥z*, so nonnegative prices and maximality imply p·a*=p·z*. Hence the unused resources have zero price value. Fixing other firms’ plans in A and changing only yj gives

p·yj ≤ p·yj* for every yj∈Yj,
p·(ω+Σyj*−Σxi*)=0.

For any x∈Pi, combine x with strictly improving sequences for every other household converging to their targets. Their sum lies in S, so passing to the limit gives p·x≥p·xi*. The same inequality holds for every x≽ixi*: local nonsatiation supplies nearby points strictly above x, hence strictly above the target, and continuity of the price functional passes the inequality to x. This last step uses actual nearby consumption points in Xi, not a derivative at an interior optimum.

The precise conclusion. Define wi*=p·xi* and

τi=p·xi*−p·ωi−Σjθijp·yj*.

Ownership shares and zero-value disposal give Στi=0. Firms maximize profit, the allocation is feasible, each target costs exactly its assigned wealth, and every weakly better bundle costs at least that wealth. This is a valuation quasiequilibrium with transfers. Its household condition permits a strictly preferred bundle costing exactly wi*. It therefore does not yet establish preference maximization on the weak budget inequality. Normalize prices by Σpℓ=1 if desired; scaling p and transfers together changes no real choice.

Cheaper-bundle upgrade. Suppose for each i there is bi∈Xi with p·bi<wi*. A strictly preferred affordable x would have p·x=wi* by quasiequilibrium. For small ε>0, xε=(1−ε)x+εbi lies in Xi by convexity, is strictly cheaper, and remains strictly preferred to the target by relative continuity. This contradicts the supporting inequality. Thus every household actually maximizes preference on its budget, and the quasiequilibrium is a competitive equilibrium with transfers.

More generally it suffices that any strictly preferred affordable x can be approached within Xi by strictly cheaper points; relative continuity produces the same contradiction. Convexity plus one cheaper bundle is a useful sufficient accessibility condition. With Xi=ℝ+L, positive assigned wealth makes the zero bundle strictly cheaper even when some prices vanish. At zero wealth the argument may fail, although failure of this sufficient condition does not prove the target is nonoptimal. The price support, access to cheaper points, authority to redistribute, and implementation of trades are separate claims.

Worked case 2: a production target and its actual owners

Goods are an input/leisure resource r and consumption c. A firm can use 0≤n≤2 units of r to produce 0≤q≤4n−n² units of c; its technology includes free disposal. The hypograph of this concave output function is convex, and its bounded generator is compact. At p=(2,1), profit satisfies q−2n≤1−(n−1)²≤1, with the unique productive optimum n=1,q=3. Net output is (−1,3) and profit is 1.

Households have endowments (3,1),(2,2), utilities r2/3c1/3 and r1/3c2/3, and firm shares (1/4,3/4). Consider the target ((10/3,10/3),(2/3,8/3)). Its total (4,6) equals the endowment (5,3) plus net output (−1,3). Target wealth is (10,4). At these wealth levels the global Cobb–Douglas demands are exactly the target; the first welfare theorem proves its efficiency. This also gives a direct check of the support theorem’s hypotheses and conclusion.

Ownership wealth before redistribution is (29/4,27/4), so the necessary transfers are (11/4,-11/4). Each target has positive wealth and the zero bundle is cheaper, so full household optimality holds. If the shares instead become (3/4,1/4), keeping the same target and technology, ownership wealth becomes (31/4,25/4) and transfers become (9/4,-9/4). Production, prices and target quantities are unchanged, but the required taxes and receipts must be recomputed. Ignoring profit income would propose transfers (3,-2), whose sum is 1; that would invent aggregate purchasing power in the stated ownership accounts.

Border’s second-welfare notes, version 26 January 2016 provide the valuation-support context. The open/noncompact separation input, ambient-versus-relative topology distinction, nonnegative-price and disposal argument, transfer construction and explicit upgrade have all been supplied here. No smooth first-order condition substitutes for the convex proof.

4. Boundary support and nonconvex technologies

Worked case 3: two different failures of decentralization reasoning

First consider pure exchange with aggregate endowment (1,1), X₁=X₂=ℝ+², u₁(x)=x₂ and u₂(x)=min(x₁,x₂). The target is x₁*=(0,0), x₂*=(1,1). It is Pareto efficient: retaining household 2’s utility at least 1 requires both its coordinates at least 1, leaving nothing for household 1. At p=(1,0), target wealth is (0,1). Every bundle weakly better for household 1 costs at least zero; every bundle weakly better for household 2 requires its first coordinate at least 1 and costs at least 1. These are genuine supporting inequalities.

Nevertheless household 1 can consume (0,t) at zero cost for any t>0 and strictly improve. It has no maximizing choice on that budget. The target is a quasiequilibrium at this price, not an equilibrium. There is no strictly cheaper bundle than its zero assigned wealth. This does not mean no other supporting price can work: at p=(1,1), assigned wealth (0,2) makes the same target optimal for both households. The boundary example separates a particular price certificate from a claim about every possible decentralization.

For a different obstruction, take one household with endowment (2,0), utility min(r,c), and full ownership of a firm whose technology is the union of the free-disposal sets below the three plans ((0,0),(-1,1),(-2,3)). This technology is not convex. The corresponding maximum utilities are (0,1,0), so the middle plan and consumption (1,1) are globally Pareto efficient. Disposal cannot increase this monotone utility.

To make the middle production plan profit maximizing, its profit pc−pr must be at least 0 and at least 3pc−2pr. Thus pc≥pr≥2pc, forcing both nonnegative prices to zero. There is no admissible nonzero supporting price, whatever value transfers are proposed. Convexifying the technology changes the economy: use weight 2/5 on the full-scale plan and 3/5 on inactivity to obtain net output (−4/5,6/5), leaving consumption (6/5,6/5) and utility 6/5, strictly above 1. A mathematical convex combination is not an available deterministic production plan in the original technology.

5. Exactly when redistribution drops out of demand

Fix a common price vector p. Suppose I≥2 households have single-valued demand maps di(mi)∈ℝL, each C¹ on a nonempty open connected income interval Ji. We suppress p temporarily. Say there is income aggregation on the product domain if Σdi(mi) is the same for any two vectors in ∏Ji with the same total income M. This is a restriction on a whole product of income possibilities, not just an observation along one redistribution path.

Common-slope theorem. Income aggregation on this domain holds if and only if di(m)=ai+bm for a common vector b and household-specific intercepts ai. Sufficiency follows by summing: D(M)=Σai+bM. For necessity, choose i≠j and change incomes by (δ,−δ), leaving all others fixed. The product’s openness allows both small signs of δ, and invariance gives d′i(mi)=d′j(mj). Because every combination of these two incomes belongs to the product, hold mj fixed and vary mi throughout Ji; each derivative is constant. All households have the same constant b, and integration on the connected intervals yields the affine forms. This proves the converse component by component, without differentiating an unspecified aggregate function.

Repeat the theorem at each price to obtain ai(p),b(p). If individual demands exhaust budgets throughout an interval, p·b(p)=1 and p·ai(p)=0, by differentiating p·di(m)=m and substituting. An inferior-good component of b can be negative on a bounded income interval; positivity of quantities there does not imply global income monotonicity. If the same affine form extends to all m≥0, with nonnegative demands and di(0)=0, then ai=0 and b≥0. Those are additional global restrictions.

The product-domain hypothesis matters. At p=(1,1), for m₁,m₂∈(2/5,3/5), set d₁₁=m₁²/4 and d₂₁=[1−(1−m₂)²]/4, with each second-good demand equal to own income minus first-good demand. These are positive, smooth, budget-exhausting paths. On the single slice m₁+m₂=1 their totals are always (1/4,3/4), yet neither first-good path is affine. This algebraic example shows why invariance on one fixed-total slice does not establish the theorem’s conclusion; it does not assert a global utility rationalization of these paths at other prices.

Worked case 4: heterogeneous shares and common subsistence slopes

At prices (2,1), first let household Cobb–Douglas shares on good 1 be 1/4 and 3/4. Incomes (8,12) produce demands (1,6) and (9/2,3), with total (11/2,9). A transfer of 4 from household 2 to household 1 produces incomes (12,8), demands (3/2,9) and (3,2), and total (9/2,11). Total income remains 20, and each aggregate bundle costs 20, but good-1 demand falls by 1 and good-2 demand rises by 2. Different Engel slopes transmit distribution into quantities.

Now use preferences ui(x)=√[(x₁−si1)(x₂−si2)] on Xi={x≥si}, with s₁=(1,0), s₂=(0,1), and income mi>p·si. Optimizing surplus expenditure gives di=si+b(p)[mi−p·si], where b(p)=(1/(2p₁),1/(2p₂)). At (2,1), b=(1/4,1/2) and the affine intercepts are ((1/2,-1),(-1/4,1/2)). The inequalities m₁>2,m₂>1 define the relevant product domain at these prices.

For incomes (8,12), individual bundles are ((5/2,3),(11/4,13/2)); after the same transfer they are ((7/2,5),(7/4,9/2)). Both aggregate to (21/4,19/2). In this explicit family a positive representative demand can be generated by √[(X₁−1)(X₂−1)] at total income M>p₁+p₂: it has total subsistence (1,1) and the same surplus budget shares. This is a proved family-specific representation. The common-slope algebra alone does not prove arbitrary aggregate demands satisfy global integrability, and this representative index is not an interpersonal welfare ordering. Individual utility rescalings leave all these demands unchanged while changing a fixed-weight sum of those utilities.

Börgers’s 14 October 2021 notes, Section 8(a), pages 35–38 distinguish income aggregation from normative representation and state affine-Engel results without their proofs. Our product-domain differentiable theorem and its boundaries are proved above; no general representative-consumer theorem is imported.

6. Arrow’s theorem with a complete finite proof

Let N be a finite nonempty voter set and A a finite alternative set with at least three members. Let ℛ be the set of all complete, transitive weak orders on A, including indifferences. A social welfare function here is an ordinal aggregation map F:ℛN→ℛ, not a numerical sum of utilities. Universal domain means every such profile is allowed. Pareto unanimity means that if every voter strictly prefers a to b, society strictly prefers a to b. Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) means that when two profiles give every voter the same comparison of a and b, including ties, their social comparisons of that pair coincide. All conditions concern one fixed voter and alternative set.

A voter d is a dictator in the precise theorem sense if, at every profile and for every pair, a≻db implies a≻Fb. If d is indifferent, this definition does not prescribe the social comparison. Finite Arrow theorem: every F with the stated domain, weak-order outputs, Pareto unanimity and IIA has such a dictator. Therefore no nondictatorial rule satisfies all those requirements. This is an incompatibility of the defined requirements, not a theorem that every institution is equally desirable or that democracy is impossible.

Call S⊆N almost decisive for (a,b) if society ranks a strictly above b whenever precisely the voters in S rank a above b and all outsiders rank b above a. IIA makes the remaining comparisons irrelevant. Call S strongly decisive for (a,b) if a≻Fb whenever every member of S ranks a strictly above b, whatever outsiders report, including indifferences. Strong decisiveness implies almost decisiveness. The empty set cannot be almost decisive, by Pareto unanimity in the opposite direction.

Propagation lemma. If S is almost decisive for (a,b), then it is strongly decisive for every ordered pair. First choose c distinct from a,b and an arbitrary profile in which all S rank a above c. Construct an auxiliary profile with a≻b≻c for S. For each outsider put b above both a,c, retaining that outsider’s original a-versus-c comparison, including any tie. Universal domain permits this weak order and any extension to the remaining alternatives. Almost decisiveness gives social a≻b; Pareto gives social b≻c; transitivity gives a≻c. IIA returns that strict comparison to the original profile. Thus S is strongly decisive for (a,c).

Similarly, take any profile where S ranks c above b. Give S the auxiliary ranking c≻a≻b, and put a below both c,b for outsiders while preserving their original c-versus-b comparisons. The a-versus-b split is exactly S against its complement, and everyone ranks c above a. Almost decisiveness and Pareto give social c≻a≻b, and IIA establishes strong decisiveness for (c,b).

These two constructions really suffice with only three alternatives. Strong decisiveness for (a,c) implies almost decisiveness there, so the same constructions give (a,b) and (b,c). Starting with (c,b) gives (c,a); starting with (b,c) gives (b,a). All six ordered pairs in {a,b,c} have now been reached. For any other alternative z, apply the same reasoning to {a,b,z}; in particular S is strongly decisive in both directions between a and z. Finally, for distinct x,y neither equal to a, apply the first construction to the almost-decisive pair (x,a) and third alternative y, obtaining (x,y). This proves the lemma on all of A, without assuming a fourth distinct alternative.

Contraction to one voter. N is strongly decisive for every pair by Pareto. Choose a strongly decisive set S of smallest cardinality, possible because N is finite; S is nonempty. If S contains at least two voters, partition it into nonempty U,V. For three distinct alternatives construct the following profile, extending it arbitrarily to the rest:

VotersStrict order
Ua ≻ b ≻ c
Vc ≻ a ≻ b
N∖Sb ≻ c ≻ a

Every voter in S ranks a above b, so society has a≻b. If society has c≻b, exactly V supports that ordered pair, and IIA makes V almost decisive for (c,b). Propagation makes V strongly decisive for all pairs, contradicting minimality. Otherwise completeness of the social weak order implies b≽c, allowing equality. From a≻b and b≽c, transitivity implies a≻c: if c≽a, transitivity would contradict a≻b. Exactly U supports a above c, so IIA and propagation make U strongly decisive, again contradicting minimality. Thus S is a singleton {d}; strong decisiveness says exactly that d is a dictator. Social ties have been handled, not excluded by an unstated assumption.

The proof requires possible auxiliary profiles, not that those profiles were historically observed. Restricted data cannot by themselves establish universal domain or IIA on all counterfactual profiles. The theorem also does not cover infinite voter sets, cardinal interpersonal input or strategic truth-telling without further work.

Worked case 5: majority, Borda and a restricted-domain escape

Five voters rank four alternatives, best first: ABCD, ABDC, BCAD, BCDA, CABD. For the pairs AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD, the counts favoring the first letter are (3,2,4,4,5,4). Hence majority has A≻B, B≻C, C≻A, and each of A,B,C beats D. The pairwise rule uses only pair comparisons and respects unanimity here, but its output is not transitive. This one cycle disproves universal transitivity of majority; the preceding coalition argument is what proves impossibility for every rule satisfying the full axiom set.

On a separate fixed three-alternative set, score Borda ballots by 2,1,0 points from best to worst. Profile R has three ABC ballots and two BCA ballots, producing totals (6,7,2) for A,B,C. Profile R′ has three ACB ballots and two BAC ballots, producing (8,4,3). Every voter’s A-versus-B comparison is unchanged, but Borda switches from B≻A to A≻B. A score total always induces a transitive weak order, yet this rule fails IIA. Moving another alternative within the same fixed set suffices; no candidate entry or deletion is needed.

A restriction on preferences can change the problem. Order a finite policy set along the real line. A voter is single-peaked with unique peak t if preferences strictly increase as a policy approaches t from the left and strictly decrease after t on the right; comparisons across the two sides may tie. With 2k+1 voters, let m be the median of the peaks, counting repetitions. If y<m, at least k+1 voters have peaks at least m and strictly prefer m to y. If y>m, at least k+1 have peaks at most m and strictly prefer m to y. Thus m beats every other policy by a strict majority: it is a Condorcet winner. This proof includes the median voter and any coincident peaks.

For policies {0,1,2,3,4,5,6}, let five voters rank by −|x−t| with peaks (0,2,3,5,6). The median is 3. Against policies (0,1,2,4,5,6), the counts (favor 3, favor the opponent, indifferent) are ((4,1,0),(3,1,1),(3,2,0),(3,2,0),(3,2,0),(3,2,0)). Three is the unique pairwise winner despite a cross-side tie. Universal domain has been restricted, so this result does not contradict Arrow. We have proved this median-winner result, not a strategy-proofness, agenda-equilibrium or general social-ordering extension.

The finite coalition and median routes are supported by Acemoglu’s MIT lecture of 6 May 2010, slides 9–19 and 26–29. The proof above fixes its own decisive-set convention, proves all propagation steps, keeps the weak social branch and explicitly includes median-equal peaks in the majority.

7. Social objectives require distributional and measurement choices

Pareto efficiency is a partial comparison: many allocations can be efficient while favoring different people. A numerical social objective adds a rule for those conflicts. A positive weighted sum W=Σαiui, αi>0, strictly increases under every Pareto improvement; therefore any attained global maximum is Pareto efficient. This follows directly from summing nonnegative utility changes with at least one positive term. It does not identify the weights or establish interpersonal units.

Individual utility changes u′i=aiui+bi, ai>0, preserve each person’s expected-utility ordering, and more general increasing changes preserve certain-outcome orders. A fixed-weight social sum generally changes its tradeoffs under different ai; additive constants alone do not affect that sum’s maximizers. To preserve its ordering after affine rescaling, weights must transform inversely, α′i=αi/ai, leaving only an aggregate constant. Specifying such a convention is an interpersonal measurement decision.

Max-min, W=miniui, also requires comparable utility levels and origins. It is not strictly increasing in every component, so its maximizers need not all be Pareto efficient: if the available utility profiles are (1,2) and (1,3), both attain minimum 1 but the latter Pareto-dominates the former. A separate efficiency refinement or the structure of a particular problem is needed. Calling an objective “social welfare” does not remove these qualifications.

Worked case 6: one frontier, three decisions

Allocate a divisible resource of 12 units between two people: x,y≥0, x+y≤12. Their declared cardinal indices are u₁=√x and u₂=2√y. Because both increase strictly in their own allocation, the Pareto frontier is exactly x+y=12: slack can improve someone, while on the frontier no coordinate can rise without another falling.

For any c₁,c₂>0, Cauchy–Schwarz gives c₁√x+c₂√y≤√[(c₁²+c₂²)(x+y)]≤√[12(c₁²+c₂²)]. Equality requires x+y=12 and x:y=c₁²:c₂², yielding a unique global maximum. Equal social weights on the declared utilities use coefficients (1,2), so the utilitarian optimum is (12/5,48/5) with objective √60. Weights (2,1) use coefficients (2,2), giving (6,6) with objective √96. These are different choices on the same efficient frontier.

For max-min let t=min(√x,2√y). Then x≥t² and y≥t²/4 imply t²≤48/5. Equality is feasible only at (48/5,12/5), where the two utility levels coincide. This particular max-min optimum is unique and efficient; that conclusion was proved from its feasible set, not assumed from the name of the criterion.

Rescale only the first individual’s index to 4u₁, leaving personal preferences and all demand implications unchanged. An unchanged equal-weight social sum now has coefficients (4,2), whose optimum is again (48/5,12/5), reversing the original distribution. A separate two-option menu illustrates the importance of utility origins for max-min: profiles A=(1,4), B=(2,2) give minima (1,2), favoring B. Replacing u₁ by u₁+3 gives minima (4,2), favoring A, without changing either person’s preference over the two options.

A defensible institutional recommendation therefore reports resources, rights to transfer, who gains and loses, the chosen welfare criterion and its interpersonal convention. “Efficient,” “the representative consumer wants it,” and “the vote selected it” answer different questions. Neither a fitted demand system nor Arrow’s impossibility theorem supplies a unique ethical weight vector.

8. Exercises

Give exact fractions and global arguments where requested. The theorem questions require the stated domains and proof steps; a plotted example or a majority cycle is not a substitute.

  1. First welfare theorem. Prove the weakly-better and strictly-better expenditure inequalities using relative local nonsatiation and household optimality. Complete the ownership-budget contradiction, stating where price signs matter and why no convexity is needed. Recompute case 1’s exchange demands and feasibility.
  2. Funded externality correction. Verify the initial private choices, incomes and utilities in case 1’s emitting-consumption economy. Recompute the compensated change, its physical and money accounts and utility effects. Which precise first-theorem premise fails? Would calling the allocation “market clearing” repair that failure?
  3. General convex support. Prove the open/noncompact separation lemma, including the boundary case. Then construct S,A for the second welfare theorem, justify ambient openness on the resource side, prove p≥0, derive the household and firm support inequalities and zero-value disposal, and show the stated transfers sum to zero.
  4. Production and ownership. Prove the global firm optimum and household demands in case 2, reconcile the target and transfers, then change ownership to (3/4,1/4). What deficit appears if profit income is omitted? Explain why a price certificate alone would not establish institutional authority to levy the tax.
  5. Quasiequilibrium is weaker. Prove the cheaper-bundle upgrade with relative continuity. Analyze both price vectors (1,0) and (1,1) in the boundary example of case 3, including zero wealth, demand existence and efficiency. Is the cheaper-bundle condition necessary for a particular target to maximize utility?
  6. Nonconvex support failure. Prove that the middle discrete production plan in case 3 is globally efficient and unsupported at every nonzero nonnegative price. Calculate the convexified alternative and explain why it is not a remedy within the original deterministic production set.
  7. Aggregation and its domain. Prove the common-affine-slope theorem for C¹ demand maps on a product of open connected income intervals, with at least two households. Derive its budget identities, recompute the heterogeneous-share redistribution in case 4, and use the one-total-slice example to explain why the converse needs its full domain.
  8. Subsistence aggregation. Derive individual and aggregate demand for the case-4 subsistence preferences at general positive prices and admissible incomes. Recompute both income allocations at p=(2,1), state the lower-income boundary, and prove the particular representative-demand construction. Does this identify a social welfare ordering?
  9. Finite Arrow proof. State the exact input/output domain and dictatorship convention. Prove almost-decisive pair propagation to every strongly decisive ordered pair and the minimal-coalition contraction. Include outsider indifferences, the case of exactly three alternatives and social ties; identify where finiteness, Pareto and IIA enter.
  10. Two aggregation rules. Recompute all six majority counts in case 5’s four-alternative profile and identify the cycle. Recompute both three-alternative Borda totals and verify the preserved pairwise information. Explain why each example diagnoses one rule while the Arrow proof addresses all rules satisfying its axioms.
  11. Restricted domain and ties. Prove the odd-voter single-peaked median-winner theorem, allowing repeated peaks and ties across opposite sides. Recompute the six contests for peaks (0,2,3,5,6). Identify which Arrow condition has changed, and which strategic or social-ordering conclusions have not been established.
  12. Normative decision and referee report, 16 points. Derive all three global optima in case 6 and the effect of rescaling u₁ by 4; explain the two-option origin shift. Then audit this memo: “The target has supporting prices, aggregate demand depends only on total income, and majority picked the plan. These facts prove it is feasible to implement and uniquely best for society.” State the missing support/upgrade, resource/authority, aggregation/welfare and collective-choice conditions. Give a defensible conditional recommendation rather than a guaranteed winner.
Complete solutions and scoring guidance

  1. If x≽ixi* cost strictly less than wi, continuity of the linear price functional would keep a relative neighborhood in Xi affordable. Local nonsatiation supplies a point there strictly above x and thus above the equilibrium choice, contradicting budget optimality. Hence weakly better costs at least wealth. A strictly preferred bundle must cost more than wealth immediately, because all weakly affordable bundles are subject to optimality. At a feasible Pareto improvement the sum of costs would therefore exceed Σwi. But Σθij=1 and Στi=0 give Σwi=p·ω+Σp·yj*. Profit maximization bounds alternative production value by this level, and p≥0 makes coordinatewise feasible consumption no more costly than available resources. The resulting strict inequality against itself is impossible. No convexity, differentiability or interpersonal sum of utilities appears.

    At p=(1,1), both endowments are worth 6. Expenditure shares (1/3,2/3) and (2/3,1/3) give (2,4) and (4,2). Each costs 6 and totals (6,6), exhausting resources. The strict concavity of the log share objective proves these are global unique positive demands. Both utility cubes are 32; their numerical equality has no interpersonal significance without an additional measurement convention.

  2. A’s endowed q is worth 2·3=6 and B’s money is worth 6. Every point on A’s budget line m+2q=6 maximizes its linear utility, so (0,3) is an optimal private choice. Given qA=3, B’s own utility rises only with its money, so it chooses (6,0). Totals (6,3) clear both markets and utilities are 6 and 6−9=−3. After the compensated agreement, A receives 2 money and uses q=2, yielding 2+4=6; B pays 2, keeps 4 money and obtains 4−6=−2. Money transfers sum to zero, money consumption is still 6, and q consumption is 2≤3. Thus B strictly gains and A is unchanged, a feasible Pareto improvement.

    B’s preference depends on another household’s emitting consumption. The welfare proof presumes all relevant effects are included in the individual commodity opportunity and own-bundle preference model. Market clearing alone says that quantities balance; it neither supplies a price for the external harm nor eliminates it. The example specifies a voluntary compensated allocation, not an enacted pollution policy or legal authority.

  3. For an open convex D excluding zero, first prove that any mixture with positive weight on an interior point and the remaining weight on a closure point lies in D: approximate the latter from D and adjust the interior component within a small ball so that the mixture equals the desired point. Let K=cl D. Nearest points to external z exist by restricting a minimizing sequence to a bounded ball and using closedness; convexity and the right derivative of squared distance give (c−z)·(k−c)≥0. If 0 is external, its nonzero nearest c directly supplies a separator. If 0 is in K but not D, choose d₀∈D; points zn=−d₀/n are outside K by the interior-segment fact. Their nearest cn satisfy ‖cn−zn‖≤‖zn‖, hence converge to zero. Unit normals have a convergent subsequence, and every projection inequality passes to p·k≥0 with ‖p‖=1. Applying this to S−int A gives the needed separation.

    Here S is the sum of strict upper contours, nonempty by local nonsatiation and convex by convex weak upper contours. The resource set A=ω+ΣYj−ℝ+L is convex and downward closed. Pareto efficiency makes S and A disjoint. Every a−ε1 has a small ambient ball below a in A, so int A is nonempty and dense in A. This avoids claiming that contours relatively open in Xi are ambient-open. Extend the separator to A by limits. Negative pℓ would let a−teℓ have unbounded positive value, so p≥0.

    Local nonsatiation places Σxi* in cl S; feasibility places it in A. It therefore maximizes value over A. Available undisposed resources a*=ω+Σyj* are coordinatewise larger, so p≥0 forces their values to coincide. This is zero-value disposal. Changing one firm’s plan while fixing the rest proves each firm’s global support inequality. Fix a strict improvement for one household and approximate the other targets by strict improvements; the separated sum gives p·x≥p·xi*. For a weakly preferred x, approximate it by locally strictly better points to extend that inequality. Finally summing τi=p·xi*−p·ωi−Σθijp·yj* gives zero by the ownership sums and zero-value disposal. These steps establish quasiequilibrium, not yet the exclusion of better equal-cost bundles.

  4. At p=(2,1), any technology point has profit at most (4n−n²)−2n=1−(n−1)². Its unique productive maximizer has n=1,q=3 and profit 1; positive prices make extra disposal unprofitable. The target bundles sum to (4,6), exactly (5,3)+(−1,3). Their costs are 10 and 4, and the Cobb–Douglas shares give demands (10/3,10/3) and (2/3,8/3). Since their incomes are positive, the zero bundle supplies the cheaper-point condition; the global share calculation independently verifies optimality and the first welfare theorem gives efficiency.

    Original ownership wealth is 2·3+1+1/4=29/4 and 2·2+2+3/4=27/4. Subtract from target wealth to get transfers 11/4 and −11/4. Changing shares gives 31/4 and 25/4 and transfers 9/4 and −9/4. Each transfer pair balances and total target wealth remains 14. Omitting profit produces supposed transfers 10−7=3 and 4−6=−2, a net receipt of 1 with no offsetting tax in those accounts. The actual firm profit and its ownership explain that unit. A price-and-transfer computation is conditional on enforceable lump-sum redistribution and available trades; it proves neither those legal rights nor actual execution.

  5. Suppose a better x costs at most target wealth. Quasiequilibrium forces equality. Given a cheaper b∈Xi, convex mixtures (1−ε)x+εb are strictly cheaper, lie in Xi and converge to x. Relative continuity keeps them strictly better for small ε, contradicting support. The same logic works for any accessible sequence of cheaper points, even without a single global cheaper-bundle construction.

    The boundary target is efficient because household 2 needs both goods at least 1 to retain min(x₁,x₂)≥1, leaving no second good to improve household 1. At p=(1,0), its wealth is 0 and every (0,t) is affordable for household 1, giving utility t without an attained maximum. Household 2’s first coordinate is at most 1 on its budget, so its maximum min utility is 1 and the target attains it. Both weak-upper-contour support inequalities hold, hence this is only quasiequilibrium. At p=(1,1), household 1’s zero budget permits only (0,0), so its target is optimal; household 2 has wealth 2 and min(x₁,x₂)≤(x₁+x₂)/2≤1, attained at (1,1). This is full equilibrium at assigned wealth (0,2), despite household 1 having no strictly cheaper point. The cheaper-bundle condition is sufficient, not necessary.

  6. The three undisposed production plans leave resources (2,0),(1,1),(0,3). The monotone utility min(r,c) reaches at most 0,1,0 on their disposal sets, respectively; the middle target is thus globally optimal for the single household and Pareto efficient. Supporting its firm plan would require pc−pr≥0 and pc−pr≥3pc−2pr. Hence pc≥pr≥2pc, which with nonnegative prices implies p=0. Every admissible price fails, irrespective of household income transfers. With only one household, balanced lump-sum transfers would in any event sum to zero for that household.

    Weight 2/5 on (−2,3) and 3/5 on (0,0) gives (−4/5,6/5), leaving (6/5,6/5), with utility 6/5. This belongs to the convex hull but to none of the original downward sets: inactivity cannot supply positive c, the middle plan cannot supply c>1, and the full-scale plan uses at least 2 of r. Treating that averaged plan as executable introduces divisibility or randomization/aggregation opportunities that were not in the deterministic model.

  7. If di=ai+bm, summation gives Σai+bM, independent of distribution. Conversely a small income transfer δ from j to i is feasible in either sign at every point of the open product and leaves the sum unchanged. Differentiating at zero yields d′i(mi)=d′j(mj). Every pair of incomes can be varied independently in the product, so holding one fixed shows the other derivative is constant on its interval; at least two households connect all derivatives to a common b. Connectedness allows integration to each affine form. From p·di(m)=m throughout an interval, differentiation gives p·b=1, and substitution gives p·ai=0. This does not force every component of b nonnegative on bounded intervals.

    At p=(2,1), shares 1/4 and 3/4 give (1,6),(9/2,3) from incomes (8,12), and (3/2,9),(3,2) from incomes (12,8). Totals are (11/2,9) and (9/2,11), both costing 20. Their differing slopes are (1/8,3/4) and (3/8,1/4). In the one-slice example, m₂=1−m₁ makes the first-good sum m₁²/4+[1−m₁²]/4=1/4, and the second-good sum is 3/4. Yet derivatives m₁/2 and (1−m₂)/2 vary with incomes. Their equality only along that slice cannot be varied independently, so it does not establish constant common slopes on a product domain.

  8. Set z=x−si≥0 and residual income r=mi−p·si>0. Maximizing √(z₁z₂) gives z=(r/(2p₁),r/(2p₂)) by the global expenditure-share argument. Thus di=si+b(mi−p·si), with b=(1/(2p₁),1/(2p₂)). Summing gives S+b(M−p·S), S=s₁+s₂=(1,1), identical to demand from √[(X₁−1)(X₂−1)] on X≥S at aggregate residual income M−p·S>0. This proves the stated representative demand for this family only.

    At (2,1), b=(1/4,1/2) and intercepts are (1/2,−1) and (−1/4,1/2). Incomes (8,12) leave surplus 6 and 11, producing (5/2,3),(11/4,13/2); incomes (12,8) leave 10 and 7, producing (7/2,5),(7/4,9/2). Both sums are (21/4,19/2), costing 20. The open individual domain is m₁>2,m₂>1. At the respective threshold the only affordable subsistence bundle is si; below it no bundle in Xi is affordable. A positive representative demand on this domain does not identify interpersonal welfare: individual rescalings leave these choices unchanged but change fixed-weight social sums.

  9. The domain consists of every profile of weak orders on a finite set of at least three alternatives, with finitely many nonzero-in-number voters; the output is a weak order. Pareto respects unanimous strict comparisons and IIA preserves any pair’s full social comparison whenever all individual comparisons on that pair, including ties, are unchanged. Dictatorship means that a strict comparison by one fixed voter controls the social strict comparison at every profile; no condition is imposed when that voter ties the pair.

    If S is almost decisive for (a,b), take a third c. For any profile where S ranks a above c, use a≻b≻c inside S and put b above both outside, preserving every outsider’s a/c comparison. Almost decisiveness and unanimity give social a≻b≻c, and IIA gives strong decisiveness for (a,c). For any profile where S ranks c above b, use c≻a≻b inside S and put a below both outside, preserving outsiders’ c/b comparisons. This gives social c≻a≻b and strong decisiveness for (c,b). Outsiders may tie the preserved pair; the auxiliary weak orders remain valid. Strong implies almost. Reapplying the two constructions yields (a,b),(b,c),(c,a),(b,a), hence all six directions on a triple. Repeat with any further alternative and the hub a to reach a in both directions from every alternative; from (x,a) and third y get (x,y). Thus three alternatives suffice and every ordered pair is reached.

    Pareto makes N strongly decisive. Finiteness permits a nonempty one of smallest size; the empty coalition is excluded by opposite unanimity. If this smallest S splits into nonempty U,V, assign U:a≻b≻c, V:c≻a≻b, outsiders:b≻c≻a. Society has a≻b. If c≻b, exactly V supports c/b, so IIA makes V almost decisive and propagation makes it strongly decisive, contradicting minimality. Otherwise completeness gives b≽c; transitivity with a≻b gives a≻c. Exactly U supports a/c, so the same argument contradicts minimality. This branch includes a social tie b∼c. Therefore the smallest set is one voter, whose strong decisiveness is the claimed dictatorship. Universal domain licenses the constructed profiles; IIA transports their pair outcomes; Pareto starts and propagates comparisons; social transitivity combines them.

  10. For AB, voters 1,2,5 favor A, giving 3. For AC only 1,2 favor A, giving 2. For AD all except voter 4 favor A, giving 4. For BC voters 1–4 favor B, giving 4. Every voter ranks B above D, giving 5. For CD all except voter 2 favor C, giving 4. Thus A beats B by 3–2, B beats C by 4–1 and C beats A by 3–2; all three beat D. Majority is not transitive at this profile, despite counting each pair independently.

    For Borda, three ABC ballots contribute (6,3,0), and two BCA ballots contribute (0,4,2), totaling (6,7,2). Three ACB ballots contribute (6,0,3), and two BAC ballots contribute (2,4,0), totaling (8,4,3). The same three voters rank A above B and the same two rank B above A in both profiles, but the social comparison reverses. Borda therefore fails IIA even though summing scores always produces a transitive weak order. The cycle and reversal are counterexamples for these specific rules. Arrow’s theorem instead proves that no nondictatorial rule on the entire stated weak-order domain can satisfy every axiom.

  11. With 2k+1 peaks in a common order, at least k+1 are at least the median m and at least k+1 are at most m. If y<m, every voter in the first group strictly prefers m by same-side monotonicity, including anyone whose peak equals m. If y>m, the second group provides the analogous strict majority. Repeated peaks only enlarge these coalitions; comparisons across sides may tie without affecting the argument. Thus m beats every distinct rival, and no other policy can also be a Condorcet winner.

    For the given distance rankings, the contest triples against 0,1,2,4,5,6 are (4,1,0),(3,1,1),(3,2,0),(3,2,0),(3,2,0),(3,2,0). The peak-2 voter is indifferent between 1 and 3, but three others strictly prefer 3, enough for an absolute majority. Restricting every preference to be single-peaked violates Arrow’s universal-domain premise. The result proves a pairwise winner on that restricted domain; it has not proved strategic truth-telling, an agenda-adjustment equilibrium or a complete majority social-ordering theorem.

  12. Strict monotonicity makes x+y=12 exactly the Pareto frontier. For positive coefficients c, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds c₁√x+c₂√y by √[12(c₁²+c₂²)], with equality only at full resource use and x:y=c₁²:c₂². Coefficients (1,2) therefore give (12/5,48/5), objective √60; coefficients (2,2), representing weights (2,1) on the original indices, give (6,6), objective √96. For max-min, t≤√x and t≤2√y imply x+y≥5t²/4. Its maximum t²=48/5 is attained uniquely at (48/5,12/5). Rescaling u₁ to 4u₁ makes an unchanged equal-weight sum use coefficients (4,2), selecting (48/5,12/5). Personal preference orders have not changed. On the separate two-option menu, minima switch from (1,2) to (4,2) when only u₁’s origin rises by 3, reversing the max-min choice.

    Illustrative referee conclusion. A supporting price can establish only quasiequilibrium unless a cheaper-bundle/accessibility argument or a direct global demand check excludes preferred equal-cost bundles. Report actual resources, profit ownership and balanced transfers, and verify authority and timely execution instead of inferring implementation from a valuation certificate. Common-income aggregation is a positive demand property on its maintained price/income domain; it neither identifies interpersonal welfare units nor provides a general globally rationalizable representative consumer. Majority selection depends on the voting rule and profile/domain; a cycle, IIA failure or a restricted preference domain must be handled explicitly. State a social criterion and its measurement convention, show who gains and loses, then make a conditional recommendation that remains subject to those institutional and informational assumptions.

    Scoring, 16 points. Award 2 each for the three global optimum derivations and 2 for the rescaling/origin analysis, totaling 8. Award 2 each for the four memo dimensions: support versus optimal choice; funded resources and authority; aggregation versus welfare; and collective-choice scope. In each dimension 1 point identifies the issue and the second supplies a relevant calculation, counterexample or explicit additional condition. Alternative ethically defensible weights earn full credit when their consequences and assumptions are stated; the rubric does not impose a favored distribution.

9. Teach-back, retention and reproduction

Teach-back. Explain why a policy memo cannot replace “Pareto efficient” with “socially best.” A full answer notes that Pareto comparisons avoid interpersonal utility scales but leave distributional conflicts unresolved; supporting prices may require transfers and a separate choice-optimality upgrade; and a social criterion or voting rule introduces additional assumptions. Use the three different efficient allocations in case 6 and the unsupported middle technology in case 3 as concrete evidence.

Delayed retention. (i) Why are case 2’s transfers (3,−2) invalid when presented as net lump sums? (ii) Where does the Arrow proof handle a tie between b and c? (iii) Can one fixed-total redistribution slice prove affine Engel curves? Answers: (i) They omit the firm’s unit profit and sum to an unfunded net receipt of 1; ownership-consistent transfers are (11/4,−11/4). (ii) The branch not c≻b gives b≽c, including equality, and a≻b then implies a≻c. (iii) No: the explicit quadratic income paths aggregate on M=1 but not on a full product domain.

Reproduce the cases. Calculate individual wealth from endowments, profit shares and transfers before calculating demand. Sum physical quantities separately from price values. For the discrete technology evaluate each entire feasible disposal branch; for the quadratic technology use the completed-square profit bound. Verify income aggregation by summing individual functions before imposing an income slice. For voting, tabulate each voter’s pair comparisons and then the totals; the table never replaces the universal coalition proof. Editorial standard-library checks independently recompute these finite witnesses and reject malformed budgets, ownership vectors and preference profiles. Their arithmetic verification is distinct from the mathematical proofs and from actual institutional or empirical validation.

10. Source limits and the next problem

The author inspected Border’s full eight-page support note and four equation-page images, and the stated MIT social-choice sections with seven proof-page images. Börgers’s aggregation section was read through actual web-extracted text; direct PDF retrieval returned HTTP 403, so no retained PDF or page-image inspection is claimed for it. The earlier MIT welfare transcript is reused within its recorded prior scope. Source notes inform definitions and proof routes; the new separation proof, exact coalition construction, numerical economies and exercises are original. Unread source books, original Arrow papers, strategic-voting extensions and infinite-dimensional welfare results are not claimed as inspected or proved.

Next. Static games and refinements replaces price-taking or sincere reported rankings with strategic choices. Equilibrium existence, welfare evaluation and incentives are distinct tasks: a mechanism that selects a desirable feasible allocation must still explain why participants would follow its rules.

Sources and further study

  • KC Border, The Second Welfare Theorem (January 2001; version 26 January 2016) — Full eight-page note: second-welfare valuation support statement, Scitovsky/resource sums, local-nonsatiation closure, relative continuity and alternative convexity definitions.
  • Daron Acemoglu, MIT 6.254 Guest Lecture: Social Choice and Voting Theory (6 May 2010) — Weak-order domain, Pareto, IIA, finite Arrow statement and decisive-coalition proof; Condorcet and single-peaked median definitions and proof.
  • Tilman Börgers, Econ 603 General Equilibrium Theory Lecture Notes (14 October 2021), Section 8(a) — Actual web-extracted income-aggregation definitions, positive-versus-normative representative-consumer distinction and common-affine-Engel statements.
  • Robert M. Townsend, MIT 14.04: Lecture 16, Fundamental Welfare Theorems (Fall 2020), official transcript — Primary lecture content on the finite first-theorem value proof, smooth supporting-price and wealth-transfer construction, and the weaker consumer condition in price quasiequilibrium.
